findings.where: Nav bar lockup (the small mark and "MMM INFRA") and the large hero mark
findings.fault: The logo has been recoloured. The wordmark is no longer the logo's blue and is set in the page's near-black. The arches are drawn in that near-black too, close to but not the logo's own grey. On this grey stone ground the full-colour logo would not reach 3:1, so this direction's only way to show the logo is a one-colour version the client does not hold.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo is meant to stay as it is (client value 7). In this look its blue is gone entirely. A one-colour version needs his yes, and nothing on the tile shows it was asked for.

findings.where: First screen: the red display headline "MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR" and the red "WRITE TO MARK" button; also every red heading (the article title, "LAID · WEIGHTY · SETTLED")
findings.fault: Headings and the one action share the same minium red. The two-line red headline is the heaviest red on the first screen, and it outweighs the smaller red button. Red therefore does not mean "act here", and the button is not the only figure in the accent colour.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor from a development bank, who scans for what to do next and finds three red things competing. It also goes against the direction's own rule, "one accent only, and it flows to the action".

findings.where: The pull quote in the article specimen, framed as a tabula ansata like the "WRITE TO MARK" button
findings.fault: One shape is used for two functions. The dovetail-handled tablet is the button's shape and also frames a static quote. The parts map flags the quote as looking actable, and a visitor learns that the ansate shape means "press me" in one place and "read me" in another.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page, who may try the boxed quote as a button or doubt that the real button is one. The house treats the button shape as reserved for actions. The direction card asks for this shape on both, so the clash goes to the founder.

findings.fault: A button looks like a link. It is underlined caps text, the same treatment as the article's "Streamlining the PPP Process…" link, so the house's link signifier is borrowed by an action that navigates nowhere.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who expects an underline to take them to another page. This is also a pattern the layout round would copy.

findings.where: "WRITE TO MARK" button and the pull quote: the triangular handles each side
findings.fault: The handles are free-standing triangles, set apart from the panel and pointing inward. They read as arrowheads aimed at the button, or as a ribbon or bow-tie banner, not as the dovetail handles of an inscription tablet. The direction's signature move does not come across.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the visitor. The shape suggests a prize ribbon or a promotion banner, a campaign-like note the brand sheet rules out (§6), instead of the Roman tablet the direction promises.

findings.where: Article specimen headline "THE WORLD'S BEST PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP LAW" (the type-pair rule "always in capitals, always tracked")
findings.fault: Every heading is in tracked Cinzel capitals, so an ordinary article title already runs to three slow-to-read lines of caps. Mark's longer real titles, such as "Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge", would become heavy all-caps blocks on article pages and in lists.
findings.who_objects: Readers scanning Mark's articles, who read long all-caps titles slowly. Angélique, too: she adds posts with whatever title Mark gives, and gets no fallback (client value 9).

findings.where: The whole tile: no photograph of Mark and no stated treatment for one
findings.fault: The look has nowhere to put the man himself. The palette is three flat colours with "no blending", and nothing says how a colour photograph of Mark, or one from his LinkedIn posts, sits on this ground.
findings.who_objects: Mark, who wants to be seen (client value 3; brand sheet §6, refreshed images). A procurement reader, too: they look for a real face on a solo advisor's site (first-visit trust item 1). The layout round would inherit the gap.

findings.where: First screen: "WRITE TO MARK" button and the nav's "CONTACT"
findings.fault: The only contact route is a mailto button. Mark's email address never appears as text.
findings.who_objects: A bank staffer using webmail or a locked-down work machine, where mailto opens nothing. They need the address itself to copy (first-visit trust item 7).

findings.where: Hero headline "MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR"
findings.fault: The interpuncts split a name and a two-word role into what reads as a list of separate words. "INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR" scans as two items, not one job title, and the lone "M" stands as a word of its own.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor reading the one strong line for who this is. The inscriptional device makes them read twice.

findings.fault: Code and an internal file path are set inline in a default monospace that is larger than the surrounding caption text. The path is internal working jargon inside a client-facing tile.
findings.who_objects: Mark, reading the tile to choose a direction. The path means nothing to him, and the mismatched face breaks an otherwise consistent type pair.
